introduction: These readings start from a denial: no heart that has recognized God apprehends His nature, and no mind can hope to fathom His essence. What can be known is the attributes, in the world and in the soul, and the One through Whom the Unknowable is made manifest; the rest of the guide is praise that keeps confessing its own failure. The denial is old and widely shared. Job, Isaiah and Paul, the Qur’an’s “Vision comprehendeth Him not”, Laozi’s nameless Tao, the Vedic poet’s “perhaps he knows not”, Plato, Xenophanes, the Mishnah and Newton all stand near it. Others press on it from different sides: Pascal doubts that reason reaches even the existence; Feuerbach thinks the image is all there is; the Nicene fathers define and John says that the Word was made flesh; Blake blesses the human form divine; Wittgenstein asks for silence; and Dickinson, who never spoke with God, is certain of the spot.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that the existence of the Divine Essence can be proved while its conditions remain unknown; Pascal says that by natural light we cannot know either what He is or if He is. What does each mean by knowing, and where exactly do they part?

“That which is in his imagination is not God.” Set this beside Xenophanes’ oxen and horses, Feuerbach’s conclusion and Rūmī’s shepherd. If every conception falls short, what distinguishes a prayer from a fancy?

The readings deny that the Essence can be incarnated and affirm that the Hidden is known through His Manifestation. How do the mirror and the sun, “the image of the invisible God” and “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father” each try to hold those two statements together?

Wittgenstein concludes that what cannot be spoken of must be passed over in silence, and the Preacher that words should be few. Why do these readings, having said that no praise can reach, go on praising at such length?
“How near art Thou to Thy loved ones”: the Báb, Isaiah, the Qur’an and the Cloud of Unknowing all join distance and nearness. In what sense can one be near to what one cannot comprehend?
The Báb hears the world of existence bearing witness; Pascal hears the silence of infinite spaces. What in a person, according to these readings, decides which is heard?

outside.why: “Too high is the All-Merciful … for the minds of men to hope to fathom His essence.” Zophar puts it to Job as a question that expects only one answer: canst thou by searching find out God?

“The birds of men’s hearts, however high they soar, can never hope to attain the heights.” Isaiah gives the distance its classic measure: as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my thoughts than your thoughts.

The reading praises One “exalted above the strivings of human hearts, however pure”. Paul, at the end of his longest argument, stops arguing and does the same: how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!

“All that man can hope to achieve is to comprehend the attributes of the Divinity, the light of which is manifest … in the world.” Paul allows the same knowledge: the invisible things are understood by the things that are made.
The attributes are manifest “in the world and within the souls of men”. The Qur’an names the same two places where the portents will be shown: on the horizons and within themselves.

“Whatsoever can be conceived by man is a reality that hath limitations.” Xenophanes made the point twenty-five centuries ago with oxen and horses, who would draw their gods as oxen and horses if they had hands.

“Its existence can be proved, but the conditions of Its existence are unknown.” Plato’s Timaeus argues to a maker of the universe and then stops at the same line: past finding out, and impossible to tell of to all men.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá holds that the existence of the Essence can be proved though nothing else about it can be known. Pascal, speaking “according to natural lights”, draws the line further back: we are incapable of knowing either what He is or if He is. What proof would survive his objection?

What a person conjures up, says the reading, “is but the fanciful image of his human condition”. Feuerbach agrees and concludes that there is nothing else: theology is anthropology. The reading says the Reality encompasses the image. What separates the two conclusions?

If Divinity “could be contained within the grasp of human mind”, it would be a mere concept. Solomon says the same of the house he has just built: the heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that knowing God means knowing “the traces and effulgences”, never the true nature. Paul’s figure for present knowledge is a dark glass: now I know in part.

However far minds fly “in the limitless space of what is knowable”, they reach only a sign. Job, having listed the works of God in sky and sea, says what the list amounts to: these are parts of his ways; how little a portion is heard of him.
The knower reaches “a sign pointing towards the Monarch”, not the Monarch. Moses asks to see the glory and is set in a cleft of the rock: thou shalt see my back parts, but my face shall not be seen.

The reading calls the Absolute a “Most Holy and Forbidden Mystery”, beyond the province of possible being. Laozi’s first lines draw the same boundary around the Tao: what can be trodden and named is not the enduring one.

“The path is barred and the quest rejected.” The Mishnah bars it too, for the sake of the Creator’s honour: better not to have been born than to speculate on what is above and beneath, before and after.
“His signs are His proof and His existence His evidence.” Newton ends the Principia on the same footing: we have no idea of the substance of God; we know him only by his contrivances of things.

“Every definition is inadequate and every depiction useless.” Wittgenstein’s last proposition draws the consequence: whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent. Yet these readings go on to pages of praise. What kind of speech is left when description is ruled out?

The person at prayer worships “God as I imagine Him”, and the reading calls that a fancy. In Rūmī’s story Moses rebukes a shepherd for just such a prayer, and God rebukes Moses: I regard the inside and the state of heart. If every image falls short, what makes a prayer true?

“All people are therefore worshippers of their own thoughts and fancies.” Blake accepts the charge and blesses it: everyone who prays in distress prays to the human form divine, and where mercy and pity dwell, there God dwells. Is that an idol or an insight?
“God being the Unnamable, we cannot refer to Him with any special names.” Moses asks for a name to carry to Israel and is given one that names nothing but being: I AM THAT I AM.
The Pen itself is “dumbfounded” and asks forgiveness for describing. The Preacher gives the rule the Pen obeys: God is in heaven and thou upon earth; therefore let thy words be few.

“The Invisible and Inaccessible can never be known.” The First Letter to Timothy has the phrase that Christian worship has kept: dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto, whom no man hath seen, nor can see.

The Essence is “exalted above and sanctified beyond every praise”. Milton’s angels praise a light that is itself invisible, whose very skirts are dark with excessive bright, before which the seraphim veil their eyes.

The question put to ‘Abdu’l-Bahá is how the unknowable Divinity is connected to “the Daysprings of Lordly splendour”. Paul’s phrase for Christ holds both sides in five words: the image of the invisible God. How can the invisible have an image?
“In the world of God there is no past, present, or future.” The psalm says it by comparison: a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past.

“The Infinite Reality cannot be said to ascend or descend.” Scripture nevertheless speaks of God in the language of place, as in this verse over which Muslim theologians long debated. How are such words to be read by someone who holds what the reading says?

Asked about the Trinity, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá begins from a Divinity that “transcends all human conception”. The Council of Nicaea, facing the same mystery, chose to define: of one substance with the Father. What does a creed gain, and what does it risk, by saying so much?

Because the Essence is beyond comprehension, God brings forth Manifestations to be “intermediaries between humanity and Himself”. The New Testament states the office and gives it to one: one mediator between God and men.
The reading reasons from the finite mind to the need of an intermediary. John’s prologue makes the same two steps in one verse: no man hath seen God at any time; the Son hath declared him.
“We are utter poverty, whereas the reality of Divinity is absolute wealth.” The Qur’an addresses all mankind in those terms: ye are the poor in your relation to Allah, and He is the Absolute.
“God hath testified, in Himself and by Himself … that there is none other God but Him.” In Isaiah the testimony is also God’s own: I am the first, and I am the last; and beside me there is no God.
“From time immemorial He hath been veiled in the eternity of His Essence.” Isaiah says it as praise, in the same breath as he says Saviour: verily thou art a God that hidest thyself.

All that is seen in heaven and earth is “naught but the manifestations of God’s Name”, while the Essence is never manifest. Hopkins sees the first half everywhere: the world is charged with the grandeur of God.
He Who is hidden “can never be known except through His Manifestation”. Philip asks to be shown the Father and is answered in those terms: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.

“The Unseen can in no wise incarnate His Essence and reveal it unto men.” The verse on which the doctrine of the Incarnation rests says that the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us. Do the reading and the verse deny each other, or speak of different things?
Contemplating the bond, the speaker is moved to proclaim “verily I am God!”; considering himself, he finds clay. Al-Ḥallāj spoke from the first of those two moments, and it cost him his life.
“When I consider my own self, lo, I find it coarser than clay!” The psalmist, under the night sky, has the same double sight: what is man, that thou art mindful of him?
“This is the night round which have circled the Nights of Power, wherein the angels and the Spirit have come down.” The words are those of the Qur’an’s chapter on the night of its own revelation.
“He it is Who is the Manifestation of Him Who is the Unknowable.” Paul in Athens takes an altar inscribed to the Unknown God as his text: whom ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.

“Whither do ye flee?” the reading asks, as the heaven of every religion is rent. The psalmist has asked it of himself and found no place, in heaven or in the uttermost sea, that is away from the presence.
“By His injunction ‘Be Thou’ all things have come into being.” The Báb’s words are the Qur’an’s: when He decreeth a thing, He saith unto it only: Be! and it is.
“It behooveth you to remain silent before His Throne.” Habakkuk sets the same rule for the whole earth before the Lord in his holy temple.
“God testifieth that there is none other God but Him.” The Qur’an’s shortest creed adds what follows from it for knowledge: there is none comparable unto Him.
This is the verse the reading quotes, in Pickthall’s English: what is seen is “the splendours which have been deposited within the realities of all things”, never the One Who sees.

The soul seeking knowledge of the Essence “is but a wanderer in the desert”. The Vedic hymn of creation ends its search for the origin in the same honesty: he verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not.
The true believer regards God as “immeasurably exalted above all the comparisons and likenesses”. Isaiah puts the challenge to the makers of images: to whom then will ye liken God?
“He hath erred grievously who hath mistaken these comparisons and likenesses for God Himself.” The Qur’an’s rule of thumb for all talk of God is a single clause: naught is as His likeness.

Of a clear mirror facing the sun one may truly say, “This is the sun”, yet “the mirror is the mirror and the sun is the sun”. This is the saying the figure is offered to explain, and the charge it drew at once: thou, being a man, makest thyself God.
God is “the one goal, towards which everything in nature yearns”. Boethius, in prison, sets the same thought to verse: all things seek their due return.

“Never shall mortal eye recognize the everlasting Beauty.” The First Epistle of John holds out what the reading withholds: we shall see him as he is. Is the difference between now and hereafter, or between two ideas of what can ever be seen?

“Can we say He is not able to confer His bounties in this century?” Emerson complained to the divinity students of Harvard that men speak of revelation as long ago given and done, as if God were dead.
“Without words, we speak, we communicate, we talk with God, and hear the answer.” Elijah’s answer came that way, after the wind, the earthquake and the fire.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes hearing the voice of God in the heart, without words. Confucius asks whether Heaven speaks at all: the seasons run and things are produced, and Heaven says nothing. Is that a different silence?
“The divine nearness is an unlimited nearness … sanctified from the comprehension of the minds.” The Qur’an gives it the most bodily measure it could find: nearer than the jugular vein.
“That which eternally endureth is the Beauty of the True One.” The Qur’an: everything will perish save His countenance.

On this Festival the Beauty “hath spoken … without veil or concealment”. The Qur’an lays down that God speaks to no mortal except by revelation, from behind a veil, or through a messenger. How does the reading’s unveiled speech stand to that rule, given what the other readings say of the Essence?
“Think ye that your allegiance to His Cause can ever profit Him, or your repudiation … cause Him any loss?” Elihu asks Job the same: if thou be righteous, what givest thou him?
“O Thou Who art the most manifest of the manifest and the most hidden of the hidden!” Augustine opens his Confessions with the same paired superlatives: most hidden and most near.
The reading’s paradox, most manifest and most hidden, is a verse of the Qur’an: He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward.
The worshipper kneels, forehead to the ground, and says: “Too high art Thou.” Isaiah in the temple sees the seraphim cover their faces, and says: Woe is me.
“No words do I find to glorify Thee.” The psalm praises and admits the limit in one line: greatly to be praised, and his greatness is unsearchable.

“Powerlessness to comprehend Thee is the essence of understanding.” Confucius defines knowledge, in ordinary matters, by the same honesty: when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it.
“Confession of shortcomings is the only means of attaining Thy presence.” Job’s last speech is that confession: I uttered that I understood not, things too wonderful for me.

Created things “can never hope to fathom the secrets even of the world of existence”. The Preacher reached that conclusion about the work done under the sun: though a wise man think to know it, he shall not find it.

If the world itself is unfathomed, asks the reading, how can the hidden Secret be apprehended? Confucius draws a practical rule from the same order of difficulty: while you do not know life, how can you know about death? Is his restraint the reading’s humility, or something else?
“The least of the signs of Thy Kingdom is … sanctified above all description.” Tennyson holds one small flower in his hand and says that to understand it would be to know what God and man is.
Through the Manifestation “the Beauty of the Unseen hath shone forth above the horizon of creation”. Paul speaks of the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in a human face.
“Thou wilt continue unto everlasting to be what Thou hast ever been.” Malachi: I am the Lord, I change not.

“A hidden Treasure … and an impenetrable Mystery enshrined in Thine own Essence.” Deuteronomy divides the hidden from the given: the secret things belong to the Lord; those which are revealed belong to us and to our children.
A praise “that hath unloosed the tongue of every stammerer in Thy celebration”. The psalmist finds strength ordained in the least articulate mouths of all.
“Every praise which any tongue or pen can recount … is debarred.” The Qur’an imagines all the trees as pens and the sea as ink, with seven seas more, and the words of God still unexhausted.

The attempt to conceive the Uncreated “is as the stirring of the drop before the tumult of Thy billowing oceans”. The psalmist says it of himself without a figure: it is high, I cannot attain unto it.
“In joy, all glory is Thine … and in sorrow, all beauty is Thine.” Job, on the day he lost everything: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.
Those who know God to be beyond their ken will “not follow every clamorous impostor that presumeth to speak in Thy name”. Jesus warns of the same voices: Lo, here is Christ, or there; believe it not.
“From eternity Thou wert … and wilt to eternity abide.” The Apocalypse: which is, and which was, and which is to come.

The prayer asks to be washed “from the stain of such doubts as have hindered the suspicious”. Tennyson, mourning a friend who doubted, will not call it a stain: there lives more faith in honest doubt than in half the creeds. Are the two speaking of the same doubt?

“Every man of insight is bereft of vision when confronted with the effulgence of the glory of Thy face.” The answer Job receives out of the whirlwind does not explain; it asks where he was when the foundations of the earth were laid.
God has revealed Himself and remains “independent of anyone besides Thee”. Paul tells the Athenians that God is not worshipped with men’s hands as though he needed any thing.
“Whoso claimeth to have known Thee hath, by virtue of such a claim, testified to his own ignorance.” Laozi: he who knows does not speak; he who speaks does not know.

For the reading every claim to have attained is a proof of failure. Dickinson never spoke with God nor visited heaven, “yet certain am I of the spot”. Is her certainty the claim the reading condemns, or another thing?

No one, on whatever wings, can “transgress the bounds which the contingent world hath set”. Agur asks who has ascended into heaven or gathered the wind in his fists, and what his name is, if thou canst tell.

The tongue of the heart objects that words “can only be adequate to such things as are of the same likeness and nature as themselves”. Tennyson says even of human grief that words half reveal and half conceal.
“How can he who is but a creation of Thy will claim to know what is with Thee?” Paul argues from the privacy of every human mind: the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God.
“The minds of the profoundest thinkers are sore perplexed.” Hamlet says it to a student of philosophy, after a night that his philosophy cannot account for.
By one Name the dispensations “have been promulgated unto the followers of all religions”. The Rig Veda: they call him Indra, Mitra, Varuna; to what is One, sages give many a title.
The prayer asks by a Name “set up above all other names”. Paul’s hymn uses the phrase of the one who took the form of a servant: a name which is above every name.

He “hath inhabited the inaccessible heights of His unity, and will continue to remain the same”. The Buddha affirms an unborn, unbecome, unmade, and gives it no will, name or throne. Is that the same affirmation with the person left out, or a different one?

The prayer asks God “to open the eyes of all that are dear to Thee”, that they not be veiled as others are. Elisha prays the same for his servant, who then sees the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.
God is “immeasurably exalted above Thy servants’ conception of Thy unity”. Xenophanes reached one god by denying likeness: neither in form like unto mortals nor in thought.

“No man’s description except Thine own description can befit Thy nature.” In Matthew the knowledge of the Father is as closely held: no one knows him but the Son, and those to whom the Son reveals him.
The Báb says that those who attribute positive qualities to the Essence “have not truly known Thee”. The Qur’an ends a chapter by clearing God of all that is attributed to Him.

If attributes are distinct from what they describe, how is God to be addressed? The Qur’an lets the worshipper call on Allah or on the Beneficent, by whichever name: His are the most beautiful names. What are names for, on the reading’s account?
“Sanctified beyond all names … How near art Thou to Thy loved ones.” The Qur’an gives the same pairing to those who ask about God: I am nigh; I answer the prayer of the suppliant.
The Báb joins the height and the nearness in one sentence. So does Isaiah: the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity dwells also with him that is of a contrite and humble spirit.

“No joy save in Thy nearness”, though “all created things are debarred from Thy sublime Essence”. The English author of the Cloud of Unknowing lives in the same two facts: He may well be loved, but not thought.
“I have found no contentment save in Thy love.” Rābiʿa asks for nothing of this world or the next, only that the everlasting beauty not be withheld from her.

“Thou well knowest the secrets of my heart, while Thy Being is inscrutable to all save Thyself.” In the Qur’an Jesus says it to God in almost the same words: Thou knowest what is in my mind, and I know not what is in Thy Mind.

“Too high art Thou for any soul to beseech the revelation of Thy gracious providence.” The prayer Jesus taught asks plainly for bread, forgiveness and deliverance. Is the Báb’s sentence a refusal to ask, or the deepest form of asking?

“Both the world of existence and the souls of men bear witness that Thou art transcendent above the revelations of Thy handiwork.” The psalm hears the first of those witnesses: the heavens declare the glory of God.

For the Báb the world of existence bears witness. Pascal looked at the same heavens with the new astronomy in mind and heard nothing: the eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me. What decides which of them a person hears?

He said: Thou wilt not see Me, but gaze upon the mountain! If it stand still in its place, then thou wilt see Me. And when his Lord revealed (His) glory to the mountain He sent it crashing down. quran-throne-verse.text: Allah! There is no deity save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him. Unto Him belongeth whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is in the earth. Who is he that intercedeth with Him save by His leave? He knoweth that which is in front of them and that which is behind them, while they encompass nothing of His knowledge save what He will. His throne includeth the heavens and the earth, and He is never weary of preserving them. He is the Sublime, the Tremendous.

rigveda-who-verily-knows.text: Who verily knows and who can here declare it, whence it was born and whence comes this creation? The Gods are later than this world's production. Who knows then whence it first came into being? He, the first origin of this creation, whether he formed it all or did not form it, Whose eye controls this world in highest heaven, he verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not

plato-past-finding-out.text: But the father and maker of all this universe is past finding out; and even if we found him, to tell of him to all men would be impossible
plato-past-finding-out.author: Plato

augustine-most-hidden-most-near.text: What, then, are You, O my God — what, I ask, but the Lord God? For who is Lord but the Lord? Or who is God save our God? Most high, most excellent, most potent, most omnipotent; most piteous and most just; most hidden and most near; most beauteous and most strong, stable, yet contained of none
augustine-most-hidden-most-near.author: Augustine of Hippo
augustine-most-hidden-most-near.caveat: New Advent’s text changes the translator’s “Thou” to “You”.

pascal-infinitely-incomprehensible.text: If there is a God, He is infinitely incomprehensible, since, having neither parts nor limits, He has no affinity to us. We are then incapable of knowing either what He is or if He is
pascal-infinitely-incomprehensible.author: Blaise Pascal

pascal-eternal-silence.text: The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me
pascal-eternal-silence.author: Blaise Pascal

milton-dark-with-excessive-bright.text: Fountain of light, thyself invisible / Amidst the glorious brightness where thou sit'st / Throned inaccessible, but when thou shadest / The full blaze of thy beams, and, through a cloud / Drawn round about thee like a radiant shrine, / Dark with excessive bright thy skirts appear, / Yet dazzle Heaven, that brightest Seraphim / Approach not, but with both wings veil their eyes
milton-dark-with-excessive-bright.author: John Milton

shakespeare-more-things-in-heaven-and-ea.text: There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, / Than are dreamt of in your philosophy
shakespeare-more-things-in-heaven-and-ea.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

analects-does-heaven-speak.text: I would prefer not speaking." Tsze-kung said, "If you, Master, do not speak, what shall we, your disciples, have to record?" The Master said, "Does Heaven speak? The four seasons pursue their courses, and all things are continually being produced, but does Heaven say anything?
analects-does-heaven-speak.author: Confucius

analects-know-life.text: Chi Lu asked about serving the spirits of the dead. The Master said, "While you are not able to serve men, how can you serve their spirits?" Chi Lu added, "I venture to ask about death?" He was answered, "While you do not know life, how can you know about death?
analects-know-life.author: Confucius

mishnah-four-things.text: Whoever speculates upon four things, it would have been better had he not come into the world: what is above, what is beneath, what came before, and what came after

rights.note: Translation published at Sefaria under a CC BY licence.

buddha-unborn.text: There is, monks, an unborn — unbecome — unmade — unfabricated. If there were not that unborn — unbecome — unmade — unfabricated, there would not be the case that escape from the born — become — made — fabricated would be discerned
buddha-unborn.author: The Buddha
buddha-unborn.year: c. 5th century BCE; written down later

rights.note: Modern translation, offered for free distribution; two sentences.

wittgenstein-whereof.text: Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent
wittgenstein-whereof.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein

rights.note: Published 1922; author d. 1951, translator d. 1957. One sentence.

dickinson-never-saw-a-moor.text: I never saw a moor, / I never saw the sea; / Yet know I how the heather looks, / And what a wave must be. / I never spoke with God, / Nor visited in heaven; / Yet certain am I of the spot / As if the chart were given
dickinson-never-saw-a-moor.author: Emily Dickinson

hopkins-gods-grandeur.text: The world is charged with the grandeur of God. / It will flame out, like shining from shook foil; / It gathers to a greatness, like the ooze of oil / Crushed. Why do men then now not reck his rod?
hopkins-gods-grandeur.author: Gerard Manley Hopkins

cloud-by-love-not-thought.text: but of God Himself can no man think. And therefore I would leave all that thing that I can think, and choose to my love that thing that I cannot think. For why; He may well be loved, but not thought. By love may He be gotten and holden; but by thought never

blake-divine-image.text: For Mercy has a human heart / Pity, a human face; / And Love, the human form divine, / And Peace, the human dress. / Then every man of every clime, / That prays in his distress, / Prays to the human form divine / Love Mercy Pity Peace
blake-divine-image.author: William Blake

newton-know-him-only-by.text: much less then have we any idea of the substance of God. We know him only by his most wise and excellent contrivances of things, and final causes; we admire him for his perfections; but we reverence and adore him on account of his dominion
newton-know-him-only-by.author: Isaac Newton

tennyson-flower-in-the-crannied-wall.text: Flower in the crannied wall, / I pluck you out of the crannies, / I hold you here, root and all, in my hand, / Little flower—but if I could understand / What you are, root and all, and all in all, / I should know what God and man is
tennyson-flower-in-the-crannied-wall.author: Alfred Tennyson
